findings.label: L1
findings.text:
Blocks that earlier versions already wrote under a directory that is now skipped are left in place, frozen, and the hint misdescribes them (`skills/project-update/update.py:1451-1454`)  in_scope: yes
why it matters: Before this change, a rule with `dirs: [vendor/x]` (or a symlinked directory pointing outside the walk) had its block rewritten on every run. Now the writer skips it and prints "rule X is not rendered there", but the old block is still in `vendor/x/CLAUDE.md` with the old rule text. The take-back never walks there, so nothing removes or updates it. Agents in that directory keep reading stale rules, and the hint tells the user nothing is there. A symlink pointing back inside the walked tree now behaves better (the take-back strips it and the result settles), so this only affects the outside-walk case.
suggested direction: When `plan.read(target)` already holds a block for that slug, say in the hint that an earlier rendering is still there and must be removed by hand.

findings.label: L2
findings.text:
On a case-insensitive filesystem (macOS default) the writer and the take-back still disagree (`skills/project-update/update.py:1408` vs `:1368`)  in_scope: yes
why it matters: Both checks compare against `RULES_SKIP` case-sensitively, but the walk sees the name as spelled on disk. With `dirs: [Vendor/x]` and `vendor/` on disk, the writer passes `Vendor`, the file lands in `vendor/x/CLAUDE.md`, and the walk prunes `vendor`. That is the same never-taken-back block this risk is meant to close.
suggested direction: Compare case-insensitively, or resolve each component to its on-disk spelling before checking `RULES_SKIP`.

findings.label: L3
findings.text:
`moved_detail` prints path names exactly as found into output an agent reads (`skills/ai-task/state.py:3762-3765`)  in_scope: yes
why it matters: Paths come from `git diff -z` with `core.quotepath=off`, so a file the suite writes with a newline or escape sequence in its name can fake a line in `verify` output, such as a fake success line. `update.py:1336-1340` (`tracked_ignored_hint`) escapes non-printable characters for exactly this reason; the new code does not follow that convention.
suggested direction: Escape non-printable characters the way `tracked_ignored_hint` does.

findings.label: L4
findings.text:
The installer's version check says "found unknown" without saying why, and refuses a valid Python whose stdout has extra lines (`bin/riskrails.js:121-126`)  in_scope: yes
why it matters: stderr is ignored. A 10-second timeout, a pyenv shim that exits 127, or a nonzero exit all give "python3 3.11 or newer is required (found unknown)", which sends the user hunting for a version problem. The `^…$` match (no `m` flag) after `trim()` also refuses a 3.12 whose `sitecustomize` prints to stdout. It fails safe, but the message is misleading.
suggested direction: Match the last line of stdout. When nothing matches, include `pv.error` / `pv.status` / the first stderr line in the message.

Released versions v2.0.2 to v3.1.0 wrote ``Run `/project-update --adopt --cleanup` to review; a human confirms the deletion.`` (checked with `git show v3.1.0:` and `git show v2.0.2:`). findings.label: I3
findings.text:
Running time and tests  in_scope: yes
- INPLACE_RE and INTERP_RE both contain nested repetition, so `ere.Compiled` searches them with `_Dfa` (NFA of 173 and 71 states), which is linear by construction. Test 18d therefore measures the DFA plus process start, not the pattern's shape. A pathological shape would fail it only if `_dfa_ok` rejected the pattern (a bounded repeat over 256, or a backreference).
- The only consumer is Python `hooks/guard/ere.py`; `tests/fixtures/guard-port/ai-path-guard.sh` is frozen. The session's `/usr/bin/grep -E` probe timed a different engine from the one that runs in production, so the bash-ERE parity question does not apply.
- On 21 adversarial inputs of 4 to 5 KB, in process with a fresh compile, every search took 0.6 ms or less and built at most 14 DFA states. Inputs included `sudo a…`, `if …`, `A=b …`, 4 KB of `'`, `(`, `$(`, mixed separators, `then perl`, `-e '-i' -e`, `-ee 'x'`, `find -exec…`, `-M x…`, `php -n…/-r…`, `fprintf` followed by 4 KB of blanks, and `writeSyn…`.

findings.label: H1
findings.text:
`inplace_edit` runs its second match on the output of `shell_segments`. That output drops heredoc bodies and treats echo/printf as plain text even when their output is piped into a shell. Writes HEAD denies are now allowed (`hooks/guard/paths.py:1255-1261`, together with `text_tool_segment` at about :172)  in_scope: yes
- Allowed on the tree, denied at HEAD, with `--only paths`:
- `bash <<EOF\nperl -pi -e s/a/b/ .ai/reports/T-1/notes.md\nEOF`
- `sh -s <<EOF …`
- `ssh localhost <<EOF …`
- `cat <<'EOF' | sh\nperl -pi …\nEOF`
- `echo perl -pi -e s/a/b/ <ctl> | sh` (also `| bash`)
- `printf '%s\n' perl -pi … | bash`
- `echo … | xargs -I{} sh -c {}`
- With every guard running (`probe_all.py`), `bash <<EOF\nperl -pi -e s/a/b/ .ai/state/current.json\nEOF` and `echo perl -pi -e s/a/b/ .ai/state/current.json | sh` are still allowed on the tree and denied at HEAD.
- why it matters: this tripwire is the only check on an interpreter writing `.ai/state/current.json`, and a heredoc to bash is an ordinary multi-line spelling, not a contrived one. The intent was to stop counting a perl that a text tool only names, but the fix also skips every heredoc body, whoever reads it. This is "allows what was denied" (behaviour 2), and no 18e case pins it. HEAD already let quoted forms through (`echo "perl -pi …" | sh`), so a determined agent had a way around before. The new misses are the unquoted and heredoc spellings a cooperative agent writes by accident.
- suggested direction: run the second match on the raw command with only the text-tool segments' own spans blanked, so heredoc bodies stay in, and never carve out a text-tool segment whose output goes to sh, bash, zsh, ssh, `xargs … sh` or `source`. Add deny cases for `bash <<EOF`, `cat <<EOF | sh` and `echo … | sh` to 18e.

findings.label: M3

- `find … -exec grep -l "perl -i" {} +`

- `git -c a=b log 'perl -i'`
- `gh pr create --body "… \"perl -i\" …"`
- `python3 s.py --what "(perl -i)" .ai/reports/…`
- why it matters: these are the commands agents use while working this risk: risk-register adds, PR bodies, and grep through xargs or find. The refusal wrongly says "writes the task's own control files". I2's wrapper residue (`sudo grep perl -i`) also goes the opposite way here: `sudo` and `time` grep are now allowed.
- suggested direction: skip the wrapper word in `text_tool_segment` (`xargs`, `-exec`, `git -C/-c <arg>`), or apply the quote anchor only after a shell-running word (`sh|bash -c`, `eval`, `$(`, a backtick), as M1's direction said. Add allow tests for these spellings.

findings.label: L3
findings.text:
B5's `php … -r` alternative in INTERP_RE extends a known false deny to php (`hooks/guard/paths.py:157-158`)  in_scope: yes
- Allowed at HEAD, denied on the tree:
- `cat > /tmp/out.md <<'EOF'\n- php -r 'echo 1;' is a one-liner; see \`x\`\n- .ai/reports/…\nEOF`
- `python3 s.py … --what "php -d k=v -r x; php -r 'x' and \`y\`"`
- Mechanism: `interpreter_text` scans the raw command, heredoc bodies and quoted arguments included. Any ` php -r ` followed by a blank sets `is_interp`, and WRITE_WORD_RE then matches any backtick or `$(`. Markdown code spans are full of backticks.
- The same shape with ` perl -e '…' ` is denied on both trees, so it is not new. Only the php spelling is new.
- why it matters: it costs one rewrite, and it fires on notes written about this very risk.
- suggested direction: apply `strip_prose` before the `is_interp` write scan, or record it alongside I1 in the risk register.

findings.label: L4

- suggested direction: match the bare word, or `/usr/bin/` and `/bin/` only.

findings.label: I5

- `GIT_EDITOR='perl -pi …' git commit`
- `GIT_EXTERNAL_DIFF=… git diff`

- Not a regression against HEAD. It belongs in the risk register, or the carve-out should refuse a segment that had an assignment stripped (`_ASSIGN`) or that carries `-O`/`--open-files-in-pager`/`--config-env`.
- `git -c core.pager='perl -pi …' log` is now denied, an improvement over HEAD.

findings.text:
The duplicate check only covers `decision open`, so afd2 is only partly closed (`skills/ai-task/state.py:3051-3058`; the other path is `cmd_ask` → `offer_decision` → `open_decision`, `state.py:1663-1671`, `state.py:2796-2807`)  in_scope: yes
why it matters: `ask` opens a "question" decision with `item["question"]` (plus context) as its text and has no twin check. Two pending questions with the same text create two open decisions with one question text. This can happen when two subagents return the same `QUESTIONS_NEEDED` item through `ask --batch`, or when a question is asked again while it is still pending. Claude's `tool_response.answers` is keyed by question text, and `hooks/guard/dialog.py:329-331` reads both as unanswerable. That is exactly the failure afd2 describes. Nothing is lost, because the questions stay on the `[Answer]:` file route, but the dialog fails and the Stop hook nags up to `stop_blocks_max`. The new `docs/hooks.md` sentence presents the rule as a `decision open` rule only, so this gap is not visible from the docs.
suggested direction: Either move the twin check into `open_decision`, where `offer_decision` already turns a refusal into "no dialog" and the file route, or record the `ask` path as the remaining part of afd2 in the register.

findings.label: L2
findings.text:
The `DECISION_DUPLICATE` message gives advice that fails when the twin belongs to another session or runtime (`skills/ai-task/state.py:3053-3057`, compare `state.py:2999-3002`)  in_scope: yes
why it matters: The twin search covers every open decision in the project. `decision show` only shows decisions bound to this session and runtime. A realistic case: session A opened a commit decision and nobody answered it, then the user starts a new `claude` (new session id) on the same tree with the same commands. Session B is refused with exit 6 and told to "send it ('state.py decision show')". That show prints "no open decision", leaving fallback on a decision that belongs to another session as the only way out. Before this change, B's new decision was appended last and worked. So this is a small usability regression for stale cross-session decisions; it is not a safety problem.
suggested direction: When the twin is not bound to this session and runtime, say so and point straight to `decision fallback --id …`, or name the twin's session in the message.

`paths.py` decodes the environment differently from the other readers (`hooks/guard/paths.py:1271`, `hooks/guard/common.py:60-61,546-548`)  in_scope: no
why it matters: `paths.py` reads through `env_b`, which decodes as latin-1. `dialog.py`, `runtime-gate.py`, `state.py` and `adopt.py` read `os.environ` (UTF-8 with surrogateescape). `.strip()` therefore treats a lone 0xA0 byte, a UTF-8 non-breaking space or 0x85 differently. Only a deliberately built value reaches this, and the outcome is safe either way: `state.py`'s own check still decides `approve`. Inside the boundary this would be LOW.
